5622.etyen:
From beta (“piece, chunk”) + suppe (“soup”), with dialectal beta as the first element. The name refers to the pieces of meat, potatoes and vegetables in the soup.
The underlying noun bete (“piece, chunk”) is inherited from Old Norse biti (“bite, mouthful; piece”). The second element, suppe (“soup”), is probably borrowed from Middle Low German suppe or soppe (“soup”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk betasuppe and betesuppe (“soup containing pieces of meat, potatoes and vegetables”).

246.etyen:
Compound of A (“the note A”) + dur (“major key, major scale”), literally “A major”.
The first element is A (“the note A”), the letter name used for the musical note. The second element, dur (“major key, major scale”), is borrowed via German Dur (“major key, major scale”) from Latin dūrus (“hard”). The deeper Proto-Indo-European origin of the Latin word is disputed.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk A-dur, Swedish A-dur and German A-Dur (“A major”).

1002998.etyen:
Derived from German Stoltenberg (“habitational surname”), originally referring to someone from one of several places named Stoltenberg. The Low German place name is traditionally interpreted as “proud hill”, corresponding to German stolz (“proud”) and Berg (“hill, mountain”). The Norwegian family is documented in Tønsberg from the 17th century and is traced to the churchwarden Henrik Monssen, born around 1590.
Compare German Stoltenberg and Danish Stoltenberg (“surnames”).
